_meta.purpose: Cross-cutting finance and accounting terms used across all sectors. Loaded by the /stock-report skill and auto-injected as hover-tooltip glossary entries on first use per section. Sector-specific terms live in the per-sector primers; per-company terms (product names, acronyms) are auto-built per ticker at draft time.
_meta.match_rules: The 'match' array lists every form Claude is likely to write that should be linked to this term. Matching is case-insensitive, whole-word, and applies to the FIRST occurrence in each section. Order entries from most specific to least so 'remaining performance obligations' wins over a hypothetical bare 'obligations' rule (none of which exist here, but the principle stays).
_meta.definition_rules: Plain English. 1-2 sentences. State what the term IS and what it is FOR. No circular definitions. No undefined jargon inside a definition (or if used, it must itself be a glossary term).

terms.definition: The cash a company has left after paying operating costs, taxes, and capital spending. What's left can fund dividends, buybacks, debt paydown, or acquisitions — it is the cash actually available to owners.
The cash a company collects from running its core business in a year, before spending on long-lived assets like factories, servers, or stores. Reported as the top section of the cash flow statement.

Money spent on long-lived assets — buildings, machines, servers, software — that produce revenue over many years. Capex is a cash outflow today; on the income statement, the cost is spread over the asset's life as depreciation.
How many cents of operating profit a company earns per dollar of capital deployed in the business. Sustained high ROIC over many years is the strongest quantitative signal of a real moat.

Net income divided by shareholder equity — how many cents of profit per dollar of book equity. Easier to inflate than ROIC because adding debt shrinks equity, so a leveraged firm can post a high ROE without being a high-quality business.

Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization. Used to compare operating profitability across companies with different debt and tax situations, but it ignores depreciation — which is a real economic cost over time, even when it isn't a cash outflow this quarter.
The price tag for the entire business: market value of equity, plus debt, minus cash on hand. What it would cost to buy the company outright, not just one share.

Enterprise value divided by EBITDA. A way to compare valuations when companies have very different debt levels and tax rates — using the whole-business price tag against a pre-financing earnings figure.

Stock price divided by per-share earnings. A P/E of 20 means investors are paying $20 today for $1 of current annual earnings — useful as a quick comparison, deceptive when earnings are temporarily depressed or inflated.

Buffett's term for what a business actually earns for its owners: reported earnings adjusted for non-cash items, less the capex truly required to maintain (not grow) the business. Closer to what an owner could pocket if she owned the whole company.

A valuation method that estimates a company's future free cash flows year by year, then discounts each one back to today using a required rate of return. The sum is what the business is worth right now.

A DCF run backwards. Instead of estimating future cash flows and getting a value, you take today's stock price as the answer and solve for the growth rate or margin the price implies. The question becomes: 'is the market assuming something believable?'

In a DCF, the value of all the cash flows beyond the explicit forecast period — the assumption that the business keeps producing cash forever after year 5 or year 10. Usually 60–80% of the total intrinsic value, and the part most sensitive to assumptions.
The blended return a company must earn to satisfy both lenders and shareholders, weighted by how much of each it uses. Typically used as the discount rate in a DCF.
The extra return investors demand for owning stocks instead of risk-free government bonds. Usually estimated at ~4–6% in US markets; the input that most affects DCF outcomes after growth assumptions.
The steady annual rate that would take you from a starting value to an ending value over N years. Useful for comparing growth across different time periods on equal terms.
One basis point equals 0.01%; 100 bps equals 1%. The convention exists so that 'rates rose 25 basis points' is unambiguous, where 'rates rose 25%' is not.

Buying meaningfully below your estimate of intrinsic value, so that even if the estimate proves too optimistic you still don't overpay. Buffett's image: a bridge rated for 30 tons; you drive 10-ton trucks across.

Revenue a company has signed contracts for but hasn't yet delivered or recognized. A backlog of guaranteed future income — the bigger it is relative to current revenue, the more visibility into future quarters.
For subscription businesses, the annualized value of all active subscriptions at a point in time. What revenue would be over the next year if no customer added or cancelled anything.

For a subscription business, the percent of last year's revenue from a cohort of customers that shows up this year, including upsells and after subtracting churn. Above 100% means the existing customer book grows even before new customers arrive — the gold-standard SaaS health metric.
Total revenue divided by user (or customer, or seat) count over a period. Tracking ARPU over time shows whether a company is raising prices or selling more to existing customers.
Generally Accepted Accounting Principles — the standardized US accounting rules public companies must follow when filing with the SEC. The 'official' earnings number.

Earnings adjusted by management to exclude items they say aren't representative — usually stock-based compensation, acquisition costs, or restructuring. Sometimes useful, sometimes a place where companies dress up numbers; always check what is being excluded.

Salary paid to employees in stock instead of cash. A real economic cost — it dilutes existing shareholders — but it isn't a cash outflow, which is why non-GAAP earnings that exclude SBC tend to look flatteringly higher.

A lease that effectively gives the lessee long-term control of the asset, like a financed purchase. Recorded on the balance sheet as both an asset (right-of-use) and a liability (future payments owed).

A shorter-term rental arrangement. Under current rules (ASC 842) it sits on the balance sheet, but the cost flows through the income statement as a single lease expense rather than split between interest and depreciation.

Restating an asset or liability at its current market value, with the change in value flowing through the income statement. Standard for trading securities; controversial for less-liquid assets where 'current market value' is itself an estimate.

How a company accounts for an investment in another business when it owns roughly 20–50%. The investor records its share of the investee's earnings on its own income statement, but not the underlying revenue.

A US public company's annual filing with the SEC — the most important document an investor reads. Covers business, risk factors, audited financial statements, and management's discussion of the year. Filed within 60–90 days of fiscal year end.
A US public company's quarterly filing with the SEC. Less detailed than a 10-K — no full audit, less narrative — but with updated financials and disclosure of material events since the last filing.

A 'newsflash' SEC filing required when something material happens between regular reports — earnings releases, executive changes, large acquisitions, lawsuits. Triggered events have a short list of required disclosure items.

The proxy statement, filed before the annual shareholder meeting. Contains executive compensation in detail, board members and their backgrounds, related-party transactions, and items shareholders are voting on. The single best document for the question 'are management's interests aligned with mine?'
Filed within two business days when an insider — executive, director, or 10%+ owner — buys or sells the company's stock. The official record for tracking insider activity.

A pre-arranged trading plan an insider sets up to sell stock on a fixed schedule, intended to insulate them from accusations of trading on inside information. Modern abuses include cancelling and re-setting plans just before favorable news.

Current assets minus current liabilities — the cash and near-cash a business has tied up in inventory, receivables, and short-term obligations to keep operating. A growing business often needs growing working capital, which absorbs cash even when profits are healthy.

An accounting line that appears when one company buys another for more than the fair value of its identifiable assets. Sits on the balance sheet at the price paid; if the acquired business turns out to be worth less, goodwill is written down — a charge that quietly signals overpayment.

A write-down of an asset's recorded value when it's determined to be worth less than what's on the books. Most common with goodwill from past acquisitions and with long-lived assets that aren't generating expected returns.

Cash a customer has paid for goods or services not yet delivered. Sits on the balance sheet as a liability — the company owes the future delivery — until earned, then becomes revenue. A growing deferred-revenue line is usually a positive sign for subscription businesses.
Revenue minus the direct cost of producing what's sold, divided by revenue. The ceiling on profitability — every cost line below gross margin (R&D, marketing, overhead) eats into what's left.
Operating income divided by revenue. What's left after all the costs of running the core business — including R&D, sales, and overhead — but before interest and taxes.
Net income divided by revenue. The bottom line — what flows to shareholders after every cost, including interest and taxes.

The annual rate used to convert future cash flows into today's dollars in a valuation. Higher discount rate means future cash is worth less today. Often equal to WACC; sometimes set as the investor's personal required return.
The minimum return a project or investment must earn to be worth doing. Often set equal to a company's WACC or to an investor's required return.
A measure of how much a stock's price moves relative to the broader market. Beta of 1 moves with the market; 1.5 moves 50% more; 0.5 moves half as much. Used in CAPM to estimate cost of equity.
Stock price appreciation plus dividends, expressed as a percent return over a period. The single number that captures what an investor actually earned.

A company using its cash to buy its own shares on the open market. Reduces the share count, which raises per-share earnings even when total earnings don't change. Value-creating only if shares are bought below intrinsic value.
Annual dividends per share divided by the current share price. A 3% yield means each dollar invested today returns three cents per year in cash, before any price change.
Total debt minus cash and short-term investments on the balance sheet. The figure used in enterprise value — what a buyer would actually owe after taking the cash with the company.

Dividends paid as a percentage of earnings (or sometimes free cash flow). A 60% payout ratio leaves 40% of earnings inside the business for reinvestment, debt paydown, or buybacks. Very high payout ratios can signal a dividend at risk if earnings dip.

The US accounting standard governing how revenue is recognized — particularly important for software and subscription companies. Sets rules on when contract revenue can be booked versus deferred, which is why RPO and deferred revenue have grown into prominent disclosures.

Shareholder equity minus goodwill and other intangible assets. The 'hard' equity — what would be left if every intangible got written to zero. Especially relevant for banks and acquisitive businesses.
